title: Credential phishing
description: Attackers impersonate exchanges, support, or wallet UIs to steal username/password, 2FA codes, or seed phrases.

title: SIM-swap / SMS 2FA takeover
description: Carrier account takeover lets attackers intercept SMS OTP and reset custodial account credentials.

title: Compromised credentials
description: Password reuse, malware keyloggers, or leaked databases expose custodial logins.

title: Custodian / exchange hack
description: Hot-wallet or infrastructure breach can drain customer funds held by the service.

title: Rogue employee / insider theft
description: Privileged staff may steal funds, leak KYC data, or abuse withdrawal tools.

title: Insolvency / bankruptcy
description: If the custodian fails, customer Bitcoin may become unsecured claims—often partially recovered or delayed for years.

title: Withdrawal / account freeze
description: Compliance holds, risk systems, or operational outages can block access to your Bitcoin indefinitely.

title: Government seizure
description: Courts or agencies can compel custodians (or concentrated federations) to freeze or surrender assets.

title: Debasement / fractional reserves
description: Custodian may not hold 1:1 reserves; you hold an IOU, not on-chain Bitcoin.

title: KYC / privacy leak
description: Identity, balances, and transaction history are visible to the custodian, hackers of their databases, and police.

title: Federation collusion
description: Enough federation members can collude to censor, seize, or steal user funds.

title: Concentrated federation jurisdiction
description: If federation operators share a jurisdiction, a single legal order can pressure the whole set.

title: Federation seed / key loss (no recovery path)
description: Unlike custodial KYC recovery, losing federation wallet seeds often means permanent loss; inheritance is hard.

title: Hot-wallet malware / clipboard hijack
description: Internet-connected devices can have malware that steals seeds, swaps addresses, or signs malicious txs.

title: Seed stored digitally / screenshots
description: Photos, cloud backups, password managers synced online, or chat history can leak the seed.

title: No / inadequate seed backup
description: Device failure without a tested backup = permanent loss of funds.

title: Unsafe seed-generation software
description: Rogue employees or malicious providers can ship RNG that leaks or constrains private keys.

title: Compromised supply chain / tampered device
description: Hardware wallet intercepted, resealed, or firmware-flashed before delivery can exfiltrate seeds.

title: Insufficient entropy
description: Weak RNG or too-few dice/coin flips produces guessable seeds.

title: User entropy instructions not followed
description: Skipping dice rolls, using too few flips, or ignoring device docs leaves entropy weak.

title: Device ignores user-supplied entropy
description: Malicious or buggy firmware may discard dice/coin input and use its own (possibly weak) RNG.

title: Audit missed critical bugs
description: Even audited code can contain unnoticed flaws in RNG, parsing, or UX that leaks keys.

title: Software changed after audit
description: Updates after the audit window may introduce new defects without re-review.

title: Audited source ≠ built/signed binary
description: You may run a binary that does not match the audited source (build pipeline compromise).

title: Forced firmware / app upgrades
description: Vendors may push updates you cannot refuse; a malicious or buggy update can compromise keys.

title: Hardware RNG / firmware seed-gen defect
description: Weak on-device entropy (historical firmware bugs) can make seeds crackable. Firmware updates do NOT fix existing seeds—you must migrate funds to a new seed.

title: Brain wallet / weak passphrase
description: Human-memorable phrases are brute-forceable; brain wallets have a long history of theft.

title: Electrum ≠ BIP39 seed incompatibility
description: Electrum generates its own mnemonic scheme, not BIP39—restoring into BIP39 wallets fails or produces different keys.

title: Dice sorting bias
description: Rolling multiple dice then sorting them before mapping biases word selection and reduces entropy.

title: Biased physical dice
description: Cheap dice may be physically biased; entropy loss is usually small but real for high-security ceremonies.

title: Unsafe / incorrect dice instructions
description: Wrong mapping tables or procedures can produce non-uniform word selection.

title: Biased own-randomness→word mapping
description: Homegrown encoding from bits to BIP39 words often has modular bias or off-by-one errors.

title: Intermediate entropy math on internet device
description: Typing dice rolls, checksums, or partial words into a phone/laptop can leak the seed via malware or cloud sync.

title: Speaking seed words aloud
description: Smart speakers, phones, and home audio can record seed phrases.

title: Cameras observing seed ceremony
description: Webcams, phones, doorbell cams, or meeting room cameras can capture written or displayed seeds.

title: Wrong CLI / unsafe checksum tooling
description: Using the wrong command or untrusted guide when computing the BIP39 checksum word can leak entropy or produce bad seeds.

title: Breaking air-gap to install software
description: Connecting an 'offline' machine to the internet to download tools defeats the air-gap.

title: Checksum word mismatch vs written seed
description: Transcription errors mean the last word you wrote doesn't match the entropy—wallet may reject or derive wrong keys.

title: Address check uses different derivation path
description: Comparing addresses across wallets that use different BIP44/84/86 paths falsely suggests backup failure (or hides real failure).

title: xpub leaks privacy / all addresses
description: Anyone with an account xpub can derive all public addresses and watch full balance/history for that account.

title: Malware on watch-only / verifier device
description: Infected online machine can show poisoned receive addresses even if the cold key is safe.

title: Address poisoning / lookalike addresses
description: Attackers craft addresses with similar prefixes or malware swaps the address shown vs the one encoded in a QR/PSBT.

title: Physical theft of seed backups
description: Paper/metal backups can be stolen, photographed, or coerced.

title: Fire / flood destroying backups
description: Single-location paper backups are lost to disasters; metal plates help but location diversity still matters.

title: Inheritance without clear instructions
description: Heirs may not find seeds, may not know passphrase/derivation, or may fall for 'support' scams while grieving.

title: Same-vendor multisig is not independent
description: Multiple keys from one manufacturer share firmware, entropy source, and supply-chain risk—one bug can hit the signing threshold.

title: BIP39 passphrase (25th word) lost / untested
description: Passphrase creates a hidden wallet; losing it or never testing recovery locks funds forever even with the seed.

title: Seed phishing / fake support / verify-wallet scams
description: Scammers pose as wallet support or 'security verification' and ask you to enter your seed into a website or fake app.

title: Single key = single point of failure
description: One compromised or lost seed controls (or loses) everything; no threshold protection.

title: Ceremony complexity → human error
description: High-security dual-computer offline protocols (e.g. Glacier-style) have many steps; mistakes can brick funds or leak entropy.

title: Multisig co-signer collusion / coercion
description: Enough independent parties can still collude, or be coerced, to move funds against your wishes.

title: Key-agent / co-signer becomes custodian-like
description: If a service holds a required co-sign key and can refuse to sign, you have reintroduced counterparty risk.

title: Credential stuffing
description: Reused passwords from other breaches are tried against exchange logins at scale.

title: Account recovery social engineering
description: Attackers abuse support/email recovery flows to take over accounts without the password.

title: Geographic / jurisdictional concentration
description: Keys or co-signers in the same country share legal process, disaster, and coercion risk.

title: Wrong network / asset (BTC vs testnet / alt deposit)
description: Sending or receiving on the wrong network (testnet, Lightning invoice confusion, or alt-chain lookalikes) can lose funds permanently.

title: Clipboard malware rewriting addresses
description: Malware silently replaces copied bitcoin addresses with attacker-controlled ones.

title: Fee urgency / under- or overpaying
description: Rushing fees under congestion can strand a tx; panic overpaying wastes satoshis. Urgency also increases address-mistake risk.

title: Destination address not verified on signing device
description: Trusting only the computer/phone display for the spend destination lets malware alter where coins go.
